2027-06-01.title: Tuesday of the second week after Pentecost · St Justin
readings: The household of God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth; the great mystery of our religion
“When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he”
2027-06-01.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Second Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Justin, philosopher and martyr (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56). June, the month of Hziran in the Syriac calendar, opens; in Kerala the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive in these days.
2027-06-01.verse: Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great: He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among Gentiles, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.
theo: June begins, and in Kerala it begins with two familiar sounds: the first heavy rain of the monsoon on the roof, and children in new uniforms walking back to school with umbrellas bigger than themselves. It is a month of beginnings, and the Church gives us on its first day a saint who spent half his life searching and the other half teaching: St Justin, philosopher and martyr. In the Epistle St Paul writes to his young co-worker Timothy, who has been left in charge of the Church at Ephesus: “I am writing these instructions to you so that, if I am delayed, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth.” Paul does not call the Church a club of the like-minded or an office that hands out certificates. She is a household, with a Father, brothers and sisters, and a table. And she is a pillar and a bulwark: a pillar holds something up so that it can be seen; a bulwark protects it so that it cannot be knocked down. What the Church holds up and protects is not her own opinion but the truth that God has revealed.

Then Paul breaks into what may be one of the oldest hymns of the Church, sung perhaps in Ephesus before he wrote it down: “Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great: He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among Gentiles, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.” Six short lines tell the whole story of Christ: the Word made flesh, his life and death, his Resurrection shown to be true by the Spirit, the angels at the empty tomb, the apostles going out to the nations, the faith of the peoples, and the Ascension. We have just walked through all of this from Christmas to Pentecost. The “mystery” here is not a riddle that cannot be solved; it is a secret that God has now opened. St Justin was a man who had looked for that secret in every school of his time. Born in Samaria about the year 100, he went from teacher to teacher: a Stoic who did not think it necessary to know God, a Peripatetic who asked first about his fee, a Pythagorean who wanted music and geometry before anything else, a Platonist whose ideas pleased him for a while. Then, as he tells us himself, an old man he met walking by the sea told him to read the prophets, who had spoken of Christ long before he came. “A fire was kindled in my soul,” Justin writes, and he found in Christ the only philosophy that is sure and profitable (Dialogue with Trypho 8, in substance).

In the Gospel the question that Justin had been asking all his life is put to Jesus directly: “Who are you?” Jesus does not answer with a definition. He points to the Cross: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own, but I speak these things as the Father instructed me.” “I am he” echoes the name God gave to Moses at the burning bush. It will be on the Cross, lifted up between earth and heaven, that Jesus shows most clearly who he is: the Son who does always what pleases the Father, and who loves to the end. Justin understood this with his life. He opened a school in Rome, wore the philosopher's cloak to the end, wrote two Apologies to the emperors defending the Christians, and the Dialogue with Trypho, a long and courteous conversation with a Jewish teacher about the Scriptures they both revered. About the year 165 he was arrested with six companions and brought before the prefect Rusticus. Asked to sacrifice to the gods, they answered that they wished for nothing more than to suffer for our Lord Jesus Christ and so be saved (Acts of the Martyrdom of St Justin, in substance). They were beheaded. The man who had searched for the truth in books gave his life for the Truth who is a person. On this first day of June, when students go back to their desks, ask St Justin to teach us to love learning and to seek in it the One who is the Truth.
outline: Ask: what am I really searching for in my studies, my work and my reading?
The Church is a home and a pillar that holds up the truth for all to see.
Six lines that tell the whole story of Christ.
Jesus shows who he is on the Cross; St Justin found him and died for him.
“Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great.”
live: Behave as one of the household (1 Timothy 3:15)
Speak of the Church today as you would speak of your own family: honestly, but never with contempt.
Look at the One lifted up (John 8:28)
Before you begin your study or work today, look for a moment at a crucifix and say: Lord, you are he.
2027-06-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, revealed in flesh and taken up in glory, you are the truth that St Justin sought in every school and found at last in the Scriptures and in your Cross. Keep your Church faithful as the pillar and bulwark of the truth, and keep us faithful as members of your household. Bless the children and young people who return to school in these days, and their teachers. Give us a mind that loves to learn and a heart that is ready, like St Justin, to confess you before all. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: St Justin wrote, around the year 155, the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist that we have: the readings, the homily, the prayers, the kiss of peace, the bread and the cup brought to the one who presides, the great thanksgiving, and the people's Amen. He said this food is not received as common bread and common drink, but as the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus. Every Holy Qurbono is that same gathering.
conn: 1 Timothy 3:16 sings who Christ is; in John 8:25 his hearers ask him “Who are you?” The Church's hymn is the answer to the crowd's question.
On the Third Sunday after Pentecost (6 June) the Church will hear Jesus say “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35); St Justin is the great early witness to that bread on the Christian Sunday.
fathers: The food we call Eucharist is received not as common bread and common drink: as Jesus Christ our Saviour was made flesh by the word of God, so the food over which thanksgiving has been made by the prayer of his word is the flesh and blood of that same Jesus (First Apology 66, in substance).
The Church, though spread throughout the world, keeps the one faith she received from the apostles as carefully as if she lived in one house (Against Heresies I.10, in substance).
magis: The Catechism quotes at length St Justin's account of the Sunday Eucharist, written to the pagan emperor Antoninus Pius about the year 155, to show that the basic shape of the Eucharistic celebration has stayed the same through the centuries.
St John Paul II names St Justin among the Fathers who, having searched in philosophy, found in Christianity the only sure and profitable philosophy, and who kept a high regard for reason.

quick: St Paul calls the Church the household of God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth.
An early hymn tells the whole mystery of Christ: revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, taken up in glory.
Asked “Who are you?”, Jesus says that when he is lifted up they will know that “I am he”; St Justin searched for the truth and died for Christ about the year 165.
2027-06-01.action: Pray today for one student and one teacher you know, as schools reopen.
2027-06-01.question: In my own search for meaning, have I let Jesus answer the question “Who are you?”

family.explain: People asked Jesus: who are you? Jesus said they would understand when he was lifted up, which means on the Cross. On the Cross we see how much Jesus loves us and how he always does what his Father wants. Long ago a young man called Justin wanted to know the truth. He asked many clever teachers, but he found the answer only when he read the Bible and met Jesus. He loved Jesus so much that he gave his life for him.
family.intention: We pray for all the children and teachers starting a new school year, that they may learn well and grow in wisdom.
family.ask: Ask: “If someone asked me ‘Who is Jesus?’, what would I say?”

illus: A retired mathematics teacher in a parish near Mavelikara kept a small exercise book from his first year of teaching, 1971. In it he had written the names of every student, and beside each name a short prayer. Every June, when the school bell rang again after the vacation, he would take it out and pray through the names, though most of those students were now grandparents. A young teacher once asked him why. He said: when I was young I thought I was only teaching sums; later I understood that I was looking after souls who were looking for the truth, and the truth is a person. Then he showed her the first page, where he had copied a line from 1 Timothy: the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the truth that every heart is looking for. As St Justin sought you and found you, let us find you in your word and in your Church. Amen.
share: The household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15). Where has the Church held up the truth for me when I was confused?
They said to him, “Who are you?” (John 8:25). How would I answer that question about Jesus in my own words?
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he (John 8:28). When did the Cross teach me who Jesus is?
pm.resp: Lord, you are the truth; lead us to you.
interc: For the Church, the household of God, that she may always hold up the truth with courage and with love.
For children, students and teachers returning to schools and colleges, that they may grow in knowledge and in wisdom.
For those who search for meaning in many places, that they may meet Christ, as St Justin did.
For Christians who suffer for their faith, that like St Justin and his companions they may stand firm.
For our farmers and for all who wait for the monsoon rains, that the rains may be good and bring no harm.
pm.close: Father, through St Justin you showed that the truth sought by the mind is found in your Son, lifted up on the Cross. Keep us in your household, faithful to the truth, and give us courage to confess Christ before all. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

term: From the Greek word apologia, a speech in defence, as in a court of law. It does not mean saying sorry. St Justin's two Apologies were written to the Roman emperors to defend the Christians against false charges and to explain what they believed and how they worshipped. From this word comes apologetics, the reasoned defence of the faith.
kidsaint: St Justin and the old man by the sea

Justin was a clever young man who wanted to know the truth about God. He went to one teacher after another. One asked for money first, one wanted him to learn music and geometry before anything else, one did not care about God at all. One day, walking alone by the sea, Justin met an old man who told him to read the prophets in the Bible, because they spoke about Jesus. Justin read them and his heart was set on fire. He became a Christian and taught others for the rest of his life, and in the end he gave his life for Jesus. Lesson: keep asking questions, and look for the answers in Jesus.

homily: Dear friends, today June begins. The rain has come, and our children are back at school. On this day of beginnings the Church gives us St Justin, a man who loved to study, who searched for the truth for many years, and who finally found it in Jesus Christ and gave his life for him.

St Paul tells Timothy that the Church is the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15). The Church is our home, and she is also a pillar that holds the truth high so that everyone can see it. And what is that truth? Paul sings it: Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great: He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among Gentiles, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory (1 Timothy 3:16).

In the Gospel the people ask Jesus, “Who are you?” (John 8:25). Jesus answers: When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he (John 8:28). We learn who Jesus is when we look at the Cross. Justin learned it from the Scriptures, and when the judge in Rome told him to sacrifice to the gods, he and his companions said they wanted nothing more than to suffer for Jesus Christ. He died a martyr about the year 165.

St Justin also left us the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist: the readings, the homily, the prayers, the bread and wine, the great thanksgiving and the Amen of the people. It is what we do in every Holy Qurbono. So today let us ask two graces: a love of learning that leads us to the truth, and the courage to confess Jesus, the Truth in person, wherever we are. Amen.
kids: Children, are you happy to go back to school? New books, new bags, maybe a new umbrella for the rain! Today we remember St Justin. He was a student who never stopped asking questions. He wanted to know: who is God? Many teachers could not answer him. Then he read the Bible and found Jesus. Jesus is the answer to our biggest questions. So when you open your books this year, say a small prayer: Jesus, help me to learn, and help me to know you better.

intro: Theme: “Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great.”

On Tuesday of the second week after Pentecost, the memory of St Justin: the Church as the household and pillar of the truth, the great mystery of Christ, and the One lifted up who answers the question “Who are you?”

points.h: The household of God, the pillar of truth
sub: A pillar holds the truth up to be seen.
A bulwark keeps it from being knocked down.
q: The sum of your word is truth; and every one of your righteous ordinances endures forever.
Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.
points.apply: When you hear the Church mocked this week, answer with one calm and true sentence instead of joining in or staying silent.

sub: Proclaimed among Gentiles, believed in throughout the world.
q: For a child has been born for us, a son given to us; authority rests upon his shoulders; and he is named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father's only son, full of grace and truth.
points.apply: Learn by heart the six lines of 1 Timothy 3:16 this week and pray them slowly each night.

points.h: “Who are you?”: the One lifted up
sub: The philosopher who died for the Truth.
q: So Moses made a serpent of bronze, and put it upon a pole; and whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.
points.apply: Spend five minutes before a crucifix this week and let Jesus answer the question: Who are you for me?

concl: The Church holds up the truth like a pillar, and the truth she holds up is a person: Christ revealed in flesh and lifted up on the Cross.
St Justin looked for him in every school and found him in the Scriptures, and gave his life for him.
2027-06-01.resolve: Love learning, seek in it the One who is the Truth, and confess him without fear.
